instructions: Read the passage and choose one answer for each question.
passage:
Nia works at a fictional community center. For years, her morning routine began with a rushed bus ride and no breakfast. She used to leave home as soon as she woke up, and she often felt sleepy during the first meeting. Now she prepares a few things the night before. Her aim is not to follow a perfect plan; she wants enough time to notice which habits suit her own schedule. One habit she wants to keep is leaving a little extra time in the morning.

Nia used to go to bed at a different time each night. She now writes down her bedtime and tries to follow a more regular evening routine. If she takes a nap after work, she records when it starts and ends. Her journal is a simple notebook, not a medical test. It helps her ask better questions about her routine, but it cannot prove why she feels a particular way.

At work, Nia used to ignore hunger until the middle of the day. She now packs breakfast and a small snack when she expects a long morning. Her appetite changes from day to day, so she does not force herself to eat the same amount. When she feels thirsty, she takes a drink. She also keeps supper simple on evenings when she returns late. Her friend chooses different foods, and Nia knows that each person has different needs.

At a cooking session, the group reads a short nutrition guide. It explains that a nutrient is a substance in food that helps the body work or grow. The guide names protein, fiber and a vitamin as examples, and says that iron is a mineral. Nia looks at the label on a loaf made with wheat, a type of grain. The guide does not promise that one meal will solve every health problem. The group asks the center for sources so that they can check what the guide says.

Nia also wants to be more active in ways she enjoys. At lunch she walks with a colleague, and she sometimes stops to stretch before returning to her desk. She takes a slow breath and gives herself a quiet minute to relax when work feels busy. She writes about her mood and stress in the notebook without assuming that one activity explains everything. If a muscle hurts or she has a health concern, she plans to ask an appropriate professional rather than guess a treatment.

After three weeks, Nia reads the notes she has made. The changes are gradual: she often leaves home earlier and has more time for breakfast, but some evenings are still busy. She decides to keep the parts of her lifestyle that fit her circumstances and change the plan when necessary. Her colleague likes the idea of recording observations without treating a short diary as proof of a cause. Nia is curious about what she will notice next month.
